title: BAUDIN. PERON, Francois & Louis FREYCINET. VOYAGE DE DÉCOUVERTES AUX TERRES AUSTRALES... sur les corvettes le Géographe,
description: BAUDIN. PERON, Francois & Louis FREYCINET. VOYAGE DE DÉCOUVERTES AUX TERRES AUSTRALES... sur les corvettes le Géographe, le Naturaliste, et la goelette le Casuarina, pendant les années 1800, 1801, 1802, 1803 et 1804. Five volumes in four, comprising two-volume quarto text with portrait frontispiece and two folding tables, large quarto atlas in two parts, containing 40 plates (23 coloured and two folding) and 14 maps, 1 cm. loss at central fold of the map of Australia, and both of the two double-page maps torn on folds, list of contents in part 2 of atlas but not in part 1 (as often), the text and first atlas in contemporary calf-backed papered boards, spines chipped and worn, joints cracked, plus 1824 Atlas Supplémentaire (25 plates, of which 8 are coloured) in original papered boards. Paris, 1807-1816-1824. The official account of the important Baudin expedition to the Pacific, the so-called “general reader’s set” comprising the narrative account and the Atlas Historique with its superb coloured plates. THIS SET INCLUDES THE EXTREMELY RARE SEPARATE ATLAS SUPPLÉMENTAIRE, ISSUED BY ARTHUS BERTRAND IN 1824, COMPRISING THE 25 PLATES ADDED TO THE SECOND EDITION ATLAS. Wantrup recorded this Atlas Supplémentaire for the first time in 2023 but was unable to provide a description of its original as issued condition. The example in the present lot may well be unique: “Copies of the first edition Atlas historique are known with the addition of the twenty-five plates new to the second. Although it does not appear to have been noted before in the bibliographies, the publisher, Arthus Bertrand, made the extra plates from the second edition available to those who had purchased the first edition atlas some years earlier. The publisher’s prospectus of 1824 noted that, in response to a number of requests, these new plates would be published as a separate atlas at 18 francs. Even seven years later a publisher’s catalogue dated January 1831 advertises the second edition “Partie historique” and “Les 25 planches inédites se vendent séparément” (The 25 previously unpublished plates are available separately). The scarcity of copies of the first edition with the additional 1824 plates rather suggests that not many took up this offer…” (Wantrup, 2023, p. 205). The official account of the Baudin expedition was published between 1807 and 1816. François Péron began preparing the narrative for publication but died before the second volume was completed. Louis Freycinet, who had become expedition commander on Baudin’s death in the course of the voyage, then completed Péron’s work. The narrative was illustrated with a two-part atlas of maps and plates, prepared by Charles Lesueur and Nicholas Petit. In preparing the narrative Péron and Freycinet ignored any contribution that Baudin had made to the expedition and failed to acknowledge the discoveries of Flinders, Grant, or Murray on the south coast, taking all the credit to themselves. The south coast, discovered by Flinders, who was now imprisoned on Mauritius, they renamed Terre Napoléon, supplying most of the features on the coast named by Flinders with French names. Consequently, it is in the French work that the first complete and detailed map of the Australian continent appeared. Assisted substantially by Flinders’s impounded charts, the French map of the continent is one of the most beautiful as well as one of the most famous of all maps of Australia. Freycinet was later to acknowledge the impropriety of their actions in appropriating what Flinders had discovered and corrected this in the 1824 second edition text and the enlarged second edition atlas. Ferguson, 449; Hill 2, 1329; Tooley, 610 – 623; Wantrup, 78a, 79a, Wantrup 82 (note). Estimate $12,000/18,000 Illustrated online at invaluable.com Lot 27. Paris, Saillant &Nyon, 1772. France was a late entrant to the exploration of the South Seas and Bougainville’s was the first officially sanctioned and supported voyage of exploration. In November 1766 Bougainville set sail from Nantes for South America. Setting off from Chile he sailed directly across the Pacific, taking possession of the Tuamotu Archipelago for France. He also took possession of Tahiti – his detailed account of the island and its people aroused great interest in Europe, where it became a significant source for the romantic vision of the South Pacific. After a long stay in Tahiti he visited Samoa and the New Hebrides. From there, assuming that these islands were Quirós’s “La Austrialia del Espiritu Santo”, he planned to sail directly west to clear up the mystery of the east coast of New Holland. Although he was on a direct course for the Queensland coast and might well have achieved his objective, the impenetrable Great Barrier Reef blocked his way and he was forced to turn north round New Guinea for Batavia. title: COOK, James. A SET OF THE VOYAGE ACCOUNTS. Comprising: HAWKESWORTH, John.
description: COOK, James. A SET OF THE VOYAGE ACCOUNTS. Comprising: HAWKESWORTH, John. AN ACCOUNT OF THE VOYAGES undertaken… for making Discoveries in the Southern Hemisphere, and successively performed by Commodore Byron, Captain Wallis, Captain Carteret, and Captain Cook... drawn up from the journals which were kept by the several commanders, and from the papers of Joseph Banks, Esq. 3 volumes, quarto, second (and best) edition, London, 1773; COOK, James. A VOYAGE TOWARDS THE SOUTH POLE AND ROUND THE WORLD, performed in His Majesty’s Ships the Resolution and Adventure in the years 1772, 1773, 1774, and 1775. 2 volumes, quarto, third edition, London, 1779; and COOK, James and James KING. A VOYAGE TO THE PACIFIC OCEAN... for making Discoveries in the Northern Hemisphere... in His Majesty’s Ships the Resolution and Discovery. 3 volumes, quarto (text) second edition, and folio atlas of charts and plates, London, 1785. Eight quarto volumes of text, and elephant folio atlas volume to the third voyage, with all plates and maps, repairs on two folding charts (first voyage), old calf, and tree calf (third voyage), uniformly rebacked, the atlas volume in uniform half calf and modern marbled boards, new endpapers, discrete contemporary noble ownership stamps on title page and final leaves, foxing and some water staining in atlas volume, Donald A. Graham bookplates. London, W. Strahan, and T. Cadell, [third voyage: H. Hughs, for G. Nicol, and T. Cadell], 1773-1785. A complete set of the official accounts of Cook’s three voyages around the world, “an essential inclusion in any collection” (Davidson). When Cook set sail on his first voyage in 1768 the world was imperfectly known. By the time of his death in 1779, in the course of his third voyage, there was little left for later explorers to do but refine the detail of what he had uncovered. His first voyage in the Endeavour, 1768-1771, was the most successful European voyage yet undertaken into the Pacific. In the course of the voyage after the Endeavour left Tahiti, Cook became the first European to land in New Zealand, headed west and made landfall on 19 April, 1770 on the east coast of New Holland, which he named New South Wales, and took possession for Great Britain. Sailing north Cook sailed inside the perilous Great Barrier Reef and passed through the strait separating New Guinea from Cape York, the first to do so since Torres. Cook’s more elaborate and better-equipped second voyage in the Resolution and the Adventure, 1772 – 1775, was sent specifically to circumnavigate the globe as far south as possible to determine once and for all whether there was any great southern landmass. In January 1773, after six months at sea, Cook became the first navigator to penetrate the Antarctic circle and, although he could not reach it, he predicted that a great landmass would be found beyond the ice barrier. Cook next undertook a series of vast sweeps across the Pacific, finally proving there was no ‘Great South Land’ by sailing right over most of it. Cook brought back a vast store of information on the Pacific and its peoples, demonstrated the value of the new chronometer in finding longitude, and proved the efficacy of a new regime for preventing scurvy. Cook’s third and final voyage in the Resolution and Discovery, 1776 – 1780, was to explore the north Pacific in search of the hoped-for North-West passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The results of the third voyage were as comprehensive and conclusive for the north and central Pacific as his first two voyages had been for the south. On this voyage Cook made what he considered to be his most valuable discovery: the Sandwich, or Hawaiian Islands. Cook landed at Kealakekua Bay in January 1779 but, after enjoying excellent relations with the Hawaiians, Cook was tragically murdered in February 1779 in a skirmish on the beach that is still not entirely understood. “Captain Cook’s three great voyages form the basis of any collection of Pacific books. Gill’s last and most renowned work, published after he had returned to Melbourne in 1864, this fine album, depicting in his characteristic style the life of the settlers and Aborigines, is widely considered to be his masterpiece. The twenty-four plates display the full range of Gill’s artistic interests. There are no urban scenes in this collection but Gill’s characteristic rural themes are all represented: the goldfields, the Aborigines, scenes of drama in the bush – whether bushrangers or lost children – as well as outback scenes of a more mundane or even pathetic nature such as “Bush Funeral” and “Native Sepulchre”, all drawn with Gill’s unfailing sense of irony and his eye for detail. Some have even seen in this work a “poignant comparison throughout between the life of the Aborigines and that of the settlers” (Wettenhall). Unlike all Gill’s earlier plate books this final and most mature work was published in a grand oblong folio format in a style comparable to the great plate books of Nicholas Chevalier and Eugen von Guérard published in the same decade. Gill’s Australian Sketchbook is also a departure from his other publications in being printed in colours by the newly-introduced technique of chromolithography. London, Printed by C. Rowarth for T. Egerton, 1803. First edition. The discovery of the Victorian coast; a foundation item for Victoria. In 1800 James Grant was instructed to sail the Lady Nelson from England to Sydney where it was to be handed over to Matthew Flinders. Grant was also instructed him to search for the western passage into Bass Strait and traverse it from west to east. This he succeeded in doing, making landfall on what is now the Victorian coast near Mt Schank and Mt Gambier, discovering the Victorian coastline west of Bass’s discoveries of 1797 and 1798. He named most of the features on the coast he discovered. On 8 December he discovered a bay but was unable to enter it and could not know what a momentous discovery he almost made: it was Port Phillip Bay. When Grant reached Sydney, Governor King sent him to chart the entire south-east coast. Bad weather, however, made this impossible and only part of Bass Strait was surveyed, from Western Port to Wilson’s Promontory. Later in 1801 Grant and Lieutenant-Governor William Paterson explored the Hunter River in the Lady Nelson, which led to the establishment of the future city of Newcastle.
